en: Thus have I heard: The Mahāassapura Sutta, Discourse at Mahāassapura, from the Majjhima Nikāya. Thus have I heard: [One time the Blessed One was staying at Mahāassapura...]
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Aṅgas at a market town of the Aṅgas named Assapura.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“‘Ascetics, ascetics,’ bhikkhus, is how people perceive you.”
And when you are asked, ‘Who are you?’, you claim, ‘We are ascetics. Bhikkhus,
since you have such a designation and such a claim, you should adopt and practice those qualities that make one an ascetic and a brahmin, so that this designation of ours may be true.
Our truth will be realized and our promise will be fulfilled.

And for those from whom we receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, their services toward us will become of great fruit and great benefit; and this very going-forth of ours [will have been well-spent].
"It will not be barren; it will be fruitful and productive.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
And what, monks, are the qualities that make one a recluse and a brahmin?"
“‘We shall be endowed with moral shame and moral dread,’ thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
But it may happen, monks, that you think: ‘We are endowed with moral shame and moral dread;
this much is enough, this much has been done; the goal of recluseship has been attained by us; there is nothing further to be done. You might then become satisfied with just that much.
“I announce to you, bhikkhus; I declare to you, bhikkhus:
‘Let not the goal of the ascetic life be lost upon you who seek that goal, while there is more to be done.
And what, bhikkhus, is more to be done?”
‘Our bodily conduct will be purified—clear, open, without flaw, and restrained.
And by virtue of that purity of bodily conduct, we shall neither exalt ourselves nor disparage others. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Now, it may be, monks, that you might think:
‘We are endowed with moral shame and moral dread; our bodily conduct is purified;
that is enough, that is sufficient; we have attained the goal of recluseship; there is nothing further for us to do’—you might, on account of just that much, fall into complacency.
I declare to you, monks, I announce to you, monks:
‘May the goal of the ascetic life not be lost for you who seek the goal of the ascetic life, while there is still more to be done.
And what, bhikkhus, is there more to be done?
‘Our verbal conduct shall be completely pure, open and manifest, without flaw, and restrained.’
"And because of that purity of verbal conduct, we shall neither exalt ourselves nor disparage others"—in this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
It may be, monks, that you think:
"We are possessed of moral shame and fear of wrongdoing; our bodily conduct is pure, our verbal conduct is pure."
‘Enough with this much; enough with this much! We have attained the goal of the ascetic life; there is nothing further for us to do’—you might reach satisfaction with just that much.
Monks, I declare to you, I announce to you:
‘Do not let the goal of the ascetic life elude you while you are still seekers of that goal, even though there remains more to be done.’”
And what, monks, is further to be done?
“Our mental conduct will be purified—clear, open, without flaw, and restrained.
And by virtue of that purity of mental conduct, we shall neither exalt ourselves nor disparage others. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
But it may be, monks, that you might think:
"We are possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing; our bodily conduct is pure, our verbal conduct is pure, and our mental conduct is pure;
this much is enough, this much has been done; the goal of recluseship has been attained by us, and there is nothing further to be done. You might then become complacent with just that much.
"I announce to you, monks; I declare to you, monks:
'Let not the goal of the ascetic life elude you who seek the goal of the ascetic life, while there is more to be done.
And what, monks, is more to be done?"
‘Our livelihood shall be pure, open, unveiled, without flaw, and restrained.
And by means of that purity of livelihood, we shall neither exalt ourselves nor disparage others. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Now, it may be, monks, that you might think:
‘We are endowed with moral shame and moral dread; our bodily conduct is pure, our verbal conduct is pure, our mental conduct is pure, and our livelihood is pure.
This much is enough, this much has been done; the goal of recluseship has been attained by us; there is nothing further for us to do’—you might find satisfaction with just that.
I declare to you, monks, I make known to you, monks:
‘May the goal of the ascetic life not be lost for you who seek the goal of the ascetic life, while there is still more to be done.
And what, bhikkhus, is more to be done?
‘We shall guard the doors of the sense faculties;’
Having seen a form with the eye, one does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.

Since, if one were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in, we shall practice for its restraint; we shall guard the faculty of the eye.
We shall attain restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose... [and so forth].
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe… having touched a tangible object with the body …pe… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.

‘Since covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow into one who dwells with this faculty of mind unrestrained, we will practice for its restraint; we will guard the faculty of mind;
we will achieve restraint over the faculty of mind. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
“Bhikkhus, it may be that you think: ‘We are possessed of a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing;
our bodily conduct is pure, our verbal conduct is pure, our mental conduct is pure, and our livelihood is pure; we are guardians of the doors of the sense faculties.
This much is enough, this much has been done; the goal of recluseship has been attained by us, and there is nothing further for us to do. You might then fall into complacency with just that much.”
“I announce to you, bhikkhus; I declare to you, bhikkhus:
‘May the goal of the ascetic life not be lost for you who seek the goal of the ascetic life, while there is more to be done.
And what, bhikkhus, is more to be done?”

‘We shall be moderate in eating; reflecting wisely, we shall take food neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for the sake of physical beauty and attractiveness, but only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body, for the allaying of hunger, and for supporting the holy life, thinking:
“Thus I shall terminate the old feeling and not give rise to a new feeling.”’
‘We shall not give rise to new feeling, and we shall maintain ourselves, be blameless,
and dwell in comfort’— thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
Now, it may be, monks, that you think thus:

“Endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing, our bodily conduct is pure, our verbal conduct is pure, our mental conduct is pure, and our livelihood is pure. We guard the doors of our sense faculties and are moderate in eating.
‘This much is enough, this much has been done; the goal of asceticism has been attained by us; there is nothing further for us to do’—you might find satisfaction with just that much.
I declare to you, monks, I announce to you, monks:”
‘May the goal of the ascetic life not be lost for you who seek that goal, while there is still more to be done.
And what, monks, is more to be done?
‘We shall be devoted to wakefulness; during the day, by means of walking and sitting, we shall purify the mind of obstructive states.’
‘In the first watch of the night, we shall purify our minds of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.

In the middle watch of the night, we shall lie down on the right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having established the perception of rising.
In the last watch of the night, having risen, we shall purify our minds of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting. It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves.
It may be, monks, that you might think:
"We are endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing; our bodily conduct is purified, our verbal conduct is purified, our mental conduct is purified, and our livelihood is purified;
we guard the doors of our sense faculties, we are moderate in eating, and we are devoted to wakefulness."
‘Enough with this much, done with this much; we have attained the goal of recluseship; there is nothing further for us to do’—you might find satisfaction with just that much.
I declare to you, monks, I announce to you, monks:
‘Do not let the goal of recluseship be lost upon you while you still seek it, as long as there is more to be done.’”
And what, bhikkhus, is further to be done?
“We shall be possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension; acting with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; acting with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
acting with clear comprehension when bending and stretching [the limbs]; acting with clear comprehension in wearing the outer robe, the inner robe, and the bowl.”
‘Acting with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; acting with clear comprehension in discharging excrement and urine;
acting with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent’—in this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
It may be, monks, that you might think:
"We are endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing; our bodily conduct is pure, our verbal conduct is pure, our mental conduct is pure, and our livelihood is pure;
we are guardians of the doors of the sense faculties, and we are moderate in eating."
“Devoted to wakefulness, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, you might think:
‘Enough is done, enough is accomplished; the goal of the ascetic life has been attained by us; there is nothing further for us to do. You should not find satisfaction with just that much.
I declare this to you, monks; I make it known to you, monks:”
‘Do not let the goal of the ascetic life elude you while there is still more to be done.
And what, monks, is that further task to be done?
Here, monks, a monk resorts to a secluded lodging—a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Then, having returned from his alms round after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor; perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending, he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells without agitation, with a mind inwardly calmed; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells as one who has crossed beyond doubt, no longer uncertain about wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.
“Just as if, monks, a man were to take a loan and apply himself to work. His work would succeed;
he would clear away the principal of his former debt and have enough remaining over for the maintenance of a wife.”
It might occur to him:
"In the past, I engaged in work after taking on debt, and those works of mine were successful.
I have cleared away the principal of my old debts, and I have a surplus remaining for the support of my wife."
Therefore, on that account, one should find joy and attain gladness.
Monks, it is just as if there were a man who was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill; he would have no appetite for food and there would be no strength in his body.
After some time, he might be freed from that affliction, his appetite for food would return, and there would be strength in his body.
It might occur to him:
"Formerly, I was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill;
food did not agree with me, and there was no strength in my body. But now I am freed from that affliction; food agrees with me, and..."
‘And there is some measure of strength in my body.
On that account, monks, he would obtain gladness and attain joy.
It is just as if, monks, a man were bound in prison.
Then, at a later time, he might be released from that bondage, safe and secure, with no loss of his wealth.
He would think to himself:
"Formerly, I was bound in prison; now I am released from that bondage, safe and secure, and there is no loss of my wealth."
On that account, one might find joy and attain happiness.
Monks, it is just as if a man were a slave—not his own master, dependent on others, and unable to go where he wishes.
At a later time, he might be released from that slavery; he would become his own master, independent of others, a free man, able to go wherever he wishes.
It might occur to him:

"Formerly, I was a slave, not independent, dependent on others, and unable to go where I wished; but now I am freed from that slavery, independent, no longer dependent on others, a free man, able to go wherever I wish.
On account of this, he would find joy and attain gladness.
“Just as if, monks, a man with wealth and property were to set out on a long journey through a wilderness.
After some time, he would emerge from that wilderness safely and securely, with no loss of his possessions.
It would then occur to him:”
‘Formerly, I set out upon a long desert road with my wealth and possessions.
Now, I have safely and fearlessly crossed that desert; there is no longer any loss of my wealth.
On account of this, he would obtain joy and experience gladness.
In the same way, monks, a monk regards these five hindrances as not yet abandoned within himself as a debt, as a disease, as a prison, as slavery, and as a journey through a desert.
Just as one regards freedom from debt, health, release from prison, the status of a free man, and a land of safety; even so, monks, a monk regards these five hindrances as abandoned within himself.

Thus, having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first *jhāna*, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

He drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion; there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
“Just as, monks, a skilled bath attendant or a bath attendant’s apprentice, having poured bath powder into a bronze basin,
would sprinkle it repeatedly with water and knead it; that ball of bath powder would be permeated with oil,
saturated with oil, both inside and out, suffused with oil, yet not leaking.”
In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion;
there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

Furthermore, monks, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.

Thus he drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration; there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of concentration.

Just as, monks, there is a pool of water with its source springing up from within it, which has no inlet of water from the eastern direction, none from the western direction, and none from the northern direction...
There would be no inlet for water from the eastern direction, nor any inlet for water from the southern direction,
and the rain-god would not pour down timely, proper showers. Yet, from that very lake, a cool stream of water would well up and completely drench,
suffuse, fill, and pervade that same lake with its cool water, so that there would be nothing in it whatsoever— altogether— [that was not so drenched].
Suppose there were a pool of water that was not touched by cool water.
In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration;
there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
Furthermore, monks, with the fading away of rapture, a monk dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness.
Thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
In this way, he drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with raptureless happiness; there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by raptureless happiness.
Just as, monks, in a bed of blue lotuses, or red lotuses, or white lotuses—some of which blue, red, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and do not rise above the water—

Those blue lotuses, water lilies, and white lotuses, nourished from within by their roots, would be completely saturated, drenched, filled, and suffused with cold water from their tips down to their roots; there would be no part of those lotuses,
whether blue, red, or white, that was not touched by the cold water.

In the same way, monks, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the pleasure that is disinterested; there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by that pleasure of disinterest.

Furthermore, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
He enters and dwells in jhāna.
He sits having pervaded this very body with a mind that is pure and bright; there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by that pure and bright mind.
Just as if, monks, a man were sitting having covered himself from head to foot with a white cloth; there would be no part of his entire body unpervaded by that white cloth.
In the same way, monks, a monk sits having pervaded this very body with a mind that is pure and bright; there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by that pure and bright mind.

When his mind is thus concentrated—purified, bright, free from blemish, rid of defilement, malleable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability—he directs his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say: one birth, two births... [as far as] thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past abodes.

Just as if, monks, a man were to go from his own village to another village, and from that village to yet another village, and from that village he were to return to his own village; it would occur to him: "I..."
‘From my own village I went to that village; there I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and remained silent thus.
From that village too I went to another village; there also I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and remained silent thus.
Thus have I returned from that village back to my own village.’”

In the same way, monks, a monk recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births... [as before] ...thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.

When his mind is thus concentrated, pure, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma...
Just as, monks, there might be two houses with doors, and a man with sight standing in the middle would see people entering the house, leaving the house, walking back and forth, and wandering about.

In the same way, monks, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, a monk sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. …pe…

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering";
he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
One understands it as it truly is:
“These are the taints,” one understands as it truly is; “This is the origin of the taints,” one understands as it truly is;
“This is the cessation of the taints,” one understands as it truly is; “This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints,” one understands as it truly is.
He understands it as it truly is.
For one who knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When it is liberated, there arises the knowledge: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Monks, it is just as if there were a lake in a mountain cleft—clear, serene, and undisturbed.
A man with good eyesight standing on the bank would see shells, gravel, and pebbles, as well as shoals of fish, moving about or staying still.
It would occur to him:
“This pool of water is clear, serene, and undisturbed. Therein these shellfish, snails, gravel, and pebbles, as well as schools of fish, are moving about and staying still.

In the very same way, monks, a monk understands as it really is: “This is suffering” … [and so on] … up to … “This is the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called a monk who is like a pool of water.
"He understands: 'There is nothing further beyond this state.
Monks, such a monk is called a "recluse," a "brahmin," a "bathed one," a "master of knowledge," a "learned one," a "noble one," and an "arahant.
And how, monks, is a monk a recluse?

"Evil, unwholesome states—those which lead to defilement, to renewed existence, which are vexatious, ripening in suffering, and leading to birth, aging, and death in the future—have been stilled by him.
In this way, monks, a monk is a true ascetic (samaṇa).
And how, monks, is a monk a true brahmin (brāhmaṇa)?"

Evil, unwholesome states—those which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and conducive to future birth, aging, and death—have been cast out by him.
In this way, monks, a monk is a brahmin.
And how, monks, is a monk a bath-graduate?

Evil, unwholesome states—those which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—have been washed away by him.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is a "bather.
And how, monks, is a monk a "knower"?

He has understood those evil, unwholesome states that are subject to defilement, conducive to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is a master of knowledge (*vedagū*).
And how, monks, is a monk a learned scholar (*sottiyo*)?

Evil, unwholesome states—those which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—have flowed out from him.
In this way, monks, a monk is a learned one (sottiya).
And how, monks, is a monk noble (ariya)?

Evil, unwholesome states—those which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—are far removed from him.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is noble.
And how, monks, is a monk an arahant?
“Evil, unwholesome states—those that lead to defilement, to renewed existence, to danger, to suffering as their result, and to birth, aging, and death in the future—are far removed from him.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is an arahant.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Mahāassapura Sutta, the ninth, is finished.
